reason: The package is a Vite build entry over the client shell library plus the browser test suite. There is no separate front-end build in Go: pages are rendered by the host and every file a page loads is embedded in the dsh binary (C1's ui/assets tree). What the entry itself contributed is carried by this area: the start sequence of dsh web and the check that the shipped web profile loads completely (DH-D-WEBAPP-1), the product files and size budget of the embedded tree (DH-D-WEBAPP-2), the install manifest and icons (DH-D-WEBAPP-4) and the keyless real-browser lane that replaces apps/web/tests (DH-D-WEBAPP-6).

The owner decided that there is no desktop application (DH-ADR-18). The Electron shell is not built in any form. Each of the 44 duties found in apps/desktop and apps/desktop-host has one answer in section 6.4 of the spec (web, command line, not applicable, or dropped with a decision), the table is enforced by test DH-T-WEBAPP-14, and section 6.5 states what a user loses.

The package is the child process Electron starts in Node mode to run the web profile and answer the shell over private IPC. In Go the host is the dsh process that dsh web starts, so the IPC ends (credential receipt, readiness, platform session, file drag, Windows console signals through a native binding) have no counterpart. Two of its duties survive in another form: the quit inspection becomes the work summary shown before a stop from the UI or the terminal, and the bounded fatal diagnostic becomes the host's crash report. Update admission (lock, drain, re-check) is not built because an update never stops a host.

The tool uploads desktop packages to one cloud vendor's object storage, raises a rollout percentage and refreshes website installers. The owner dropped the vendor release publisher: releases are GitHub release assets produced by the release workflow, and there are no installers. Its durable rules (separate credentials for building and publishing, verify before upload, artifacts before manifest) are kept as requirements DH-LIB-COS-R1 to R5 of the library specification.

The tool writes a plugin market index from a list of npm packages and Git repositories for the Discover page. The owner decided that plugins are installed from local directories with no download or discovery, so there is no market and no index to generate. If a registry is added later, the generator's safety rules (read only, bounded sizes, integrity checks, Git hooks disabled) are recorded as the starting point in DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8.

The marker is a dated TODO to remove legacy version-mode aliases from the script that derives the desktop CI build version. It exists only because of upstream's desktop build process: the Go project has no desktop build (DH-ADR-18) and a release reads its version from the tag through the Go build information.

title: Desktop: account sign-in is not connected in the welcome window, and Windows window material still needs platform QA
Desktop: release signing, notarization, update hosting and installed-update qualification require the production release environment
Desktop: dependency lifecycle scripts follow pnpm's build permissions with no separate approval dialog
Desktop and the command line share product data under one home while keeping separate executable packages, plugin activation and lockfiles
Desktop: on a win32-arm64 host the bundled runtime payload is still x64, so the workspace-dependencies tool can reject it
Publisher: a private tool with no standalone artifact; workflow checkouts must carry the shared lockfile and workspace metadata
Publisher: its isolated-install and preflight tests neither authorize a production write nor prove that an installer upgrades a real client
Market generator: GitHub token permissions and API rate limits can silently remove metric counts
Market generator: cached package data does not make a run offline; every run requests sources and metrics
Market generator: a Git server must allow fetching a commit by its SHA, otherwise a moved ref fails the run
Market generator: registry tokens from .npmrc are not applied, so only public registries work
Market generator: Git never prompts for credentials; a private repository needs a helper or an ssh agent
Web browser tests live in two TypeScript compiler programs by convention: each scenario must be listed in both and must not import client packages, and nothing enforces it

reason: The limit describes the Electron welcome window's sign-in button and the native window material on Windows. Neither exists in the Go design: there is no desktop application (DH-ADR-18), first run is a host-rendered setup page (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-3), and account sign-in opens in the system browser.

Part of the limit is removed: update hosting and installed-update qualification no longer need the production environment, because dsh update is qualified against a private feed with a test update key (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-1, DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3). The other part remains: a macOS Developer ID signature with notarization and a Windows code signature can only be produced with the real certificates inside the protected release environment.
justification: Platform signatures vouch for the publisher, so they cannot be produced or fully rehearsed outside the environment that holds the certificates; DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-2 keeps signing in the tag-triggered release workflow on purpose, and the certificates themselves are an organisational matter the owner left open. No design change removes this.

reason: The limit exists only because desktop plugins are npm packages installed by a bundled pnpm whose lifecycle scripts may run. In the Go design a plugin is a local directory that runs as its own process under operator grants (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-4); nothing installs dependencies or runs install scripts.

The split existed because two installations (the Electron application and an npm-installed dsh) carried different package trees while sharing one data root. The Go product is one binary with no package state, and several dsh processes share one harness home under per-session leases (DH-ADR-12), so there is nothing to keep separate and no reserved desktop profile.

The limit is about the architecture of the bundled Python, Node and pnpm payload. No payload is built or shipped in the Go design (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8, DH-ADR-18), and the dsh binary is cross-compiled per target including windows-arm64.
The limit describes how the private publisher tool is installed from the pnpm workspace. The tool is not built (DH-ADR-24, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8); publication is a job of the release workflow.

The limit states what the publisher's own tests do not prove about installers. The publisher is not built and there is no installer (DH-ADR-24, DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-3); whether a real binary is replaced correctly is proven by the dsh update scenarios of the update library specification.
A limit of the plugin market index generator's GitHub metric requests. The generator is not built because there is no plugin market or discovery (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).
A limit of the plugin market index generator's cache: it still needs the network on every run. The generator is not built (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).
A limit of how the plugin market index generator fetches Git commits. The generator is not built (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).
A limit of the plugin market index generator's npm registry access. The generator is not built and the Go design reads no npm registry (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).
A limit of the plugin market index generator's Git credential handling. The generator is not built (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).

The rule exists only because of TypeScript: host and client code merge the cordis Context type under the same keys with different services, so one compiler program cannot hold both and browser tests must be listed in two projects by hand. Go has one module and one type system. The one import boundary that remains (which packages may import the browser driver) is a test, requirement DH-LIB-PLAYWRIGHT-R6.

Read in full. The first verdict assumed a Go webview shell; the owner removed it (DH-ADR-18), so no shell, no reserved desktop profile and no bundled pnpm exist. The note's goals are met differently: nothing has to be installed because the host and the UI are one binary; the release identity rule (shell, client and host qualified as one version) holds by construction because the UI is embedded (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-1); and the one update flow is dsh update (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3). Two lessons are kept: a release build ignores development resource overrides, and a release is signed or it is not a release (DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-2).

The note materialises the npm production graph in the application so that nothing is installed at first start, and keeps user plugins in the profile across upgrades. In Go there is no package graph: the binary is the runtime (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-1). The part worth keeping holds without a mechanism: plugins are local directories outside the binary (DH-ADR-13), disabling one keeps its files and configuration, and an update replaces one file and never touches the harness home.

The separate native welcome window with its own React bundle and blurred material is not built. First run is a setup page rendered by the host in the same UI (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-3, DH-D-WEBAPP-3). The note's hard-won rules are kept: credential onboarding has exactly one owner so that a skip is not followed by a second dialog; a skip is valid for one process and is never stored; and the setup path uses the product's real callbacks, not a preview. The native blur is a recorded loss.

The first verdict (ported, as the wrapper of DH-ADR-3) no longer holds: DH-ADR-18 removed the native shell that would have wrapped the web application. The note's rule, that there is one composition and one serving path and never a second backend for a second client, is satisfied by construction because the browser on the HTTP path is the only kind of UI client. Its native directory dialog is replaced by the host's directory browser; the duty table records each remaining native control.

There is no native dialog. The goal, a recovery path that does not depend on the component that failed, is met by one diagnostic on standard error with a crash-report file from the web host area, and in the browser by a host-not-reachable state shown from markup the page already holds (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4, DH-D-WEBAPP-5). Lessons kept: the first report claims the presentation and later ones go to the log; recovery never resets configuration by itself. Two gaps are reported in the spec: no finished specification defines the start without plugins, and upstream's option to set the profile patch aside with its exact bytes has no counterpart yet.

The first verdict (ported to a Go shell) no longer holds. The note exists because on Windows closing the last window quits the host, so a close shortcut with a stale target must never fall back to the window. In the Go product the browser owns its close-tab key and a page cannot take it, and closing a tab or every tab stops nothing (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4), so the danger is gone. The lesson is kept as a rule for UI shortcuts: a command whose target is stale does nothing.

The note partitions Electron browser storage per account for embedded vendor Platform pages. The owner dropped embedded sign-in and account pages (DH-ADR-18): they open in the system browser, whose own profile keeps a site's preferences. There is no embedded view whose storage could be partitioned.

There is no window to hide and no tray. The outcome the note wanted is kept: closing the UI never stops running work, because the host is a separate process from every tab, and stopping the host asks first when agents, queued input, jobs or armed schedules would be interrupted (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4, DH-D-WEBAPP-5, with the command-line area's stop function). Lessons kept: an inspection that does not answer in two seconds counts as work running; a second request joins the open question; an operating-system shutdown never waits for an answer. The tray icon is a recorded loss.

The shell's own settings file existed because the shell had to work before the host started. With one process the split collapses: the update channel is ordinary host configuration and a flag of dsh update (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3), and the test-authentication switch disappears with the mandatory-update service. The note's rule is kept where it still bites: a function that must work without a composed tree (dsh update, the fatal diagnostic) reads flags or one file directly and never component configuration.

The first verdict (ported) is overruled. The note ships Python, Node.js, pnpm and data and Office libraries as a desktop payload. With no desktop application nothing is bundled or downloaded (DH-ADR-18, DH-O-10), office work uses an operator-installed LibreOffice (DH-ADR-20), and the context area already dropped the tool that reports the payload. The loss is stated in section 6.5: an agent on a machine without these programs cannot use them. The note's restraint is kept: dsh never changes PATH or package-manager configuration.

The note replaces the sidebar browser's iframe with an Electron webview guest that has per-workspace storage. The owner dropped the embedded browser pane (DH-ADR-18): a web page has no guest surface, no storage partition and no request filter, and an iframe would share the tab's cookie jar. Links open in a new tab of the system browser.

Kept as decided upstream: four install icons (192 and 512 pixel, a maskable 512 and a 180 pixel Apple touch icon), display standalone, relative start address and scope, and no service worker. They are committed files in the embedded asset tree, served without a credential because a browser fetches a manifest without cookies. The browser check of the maskable icon's safe area is kept as part of scenario DH-E-WEBAPP-4. The manifest itself is proposed as an inference for the owner to confirm (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-5). The TypeScript icon rendering script is upstream build tooling and is not carried over.

The proposal defines a vendor endpoint that can block the desktop application until it updates. The owner dropped the mandatory-update service (DH-ADR-24): update checks are ordinary and optional, and nothing can block a local tool remotely.

The first verdict kept the deferral. Read against DH-ADR-18 the candidates have no subject: independent desktop revisions need a desktop package; install-on-next-launch and replacing a pending update need a download that is kept pending, and dsh update keeps none (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3). The one piece with a future, a stable and a pre-release channel, is already in the update design, and full SemVer comparison is kept so nothing here is ruled out later.

The policy is adopted in a changed form. Discovery is optional and off until the operator turns it on, and only produces a notice in the web UI (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-2, DH-D-WEBAPP-5); the download and swap are the dsh update command; an update never stops or restarts a running host, so the task-safe shutdown the proposal qualifies is not needed. The CDN and capacity items do not apply to GitHub release assets (DH-ADR-24). Lesson kept: approval for one version is never turned into installing another, so the command names the exact version before it asks.

The note notarises an update archive and a disk image in parallel from two isolated copies of one application bundle. The Go release has no bundle and no disk image: one dsh binary per architecture is signed and notarised once (DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-2), and a bare executable cannot carry a stapled ticket. The lesson that still applies to any release pipeline is kept: a step that mutates an artifact works on its own copy, and every lane settles before cleanup.

Upstream build process: a cache that avoids re-signing thousands of unchanged bundled runtime files (Python, LibreOffice) with the hardware token on every desktop build. The Go release signs two executables on Windows and bundles no runtime, so there is nothing to cache.

The failure analysis holds unchanged for dsh.exe: a combined sign-and-timestamp command reports a timestamp-server error as a signing failure, and retrying it uses the private key a second time. The rule is kept as requirement DH-LIB-ELECTRONBUILDER-R6 under DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-2: a private-key operation is never retried automatically, and a timestamp request is retried at most three times. Whether the release tool's signing hook can run the two phases separately was not verified and is left to the toolchain.

npm tooling: the note removes code that pruned node_modules, dependency declarations and the lockfile inside the desktop profile. A Go profile holds configuration only and there is no desktop profile.

The method is kept: a keyless, deterministic lane in which a real browser drives the real product while recorded model output is replayed, with failure on any page error, connection-loss warning or unconsumed recording (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-6, DH-D-WEBAPP-6). Changed after reading the note: the lane drives the built dsh binary, not an in-process composition, which removes the gap the note itself names between its scaffold and the shipped command; the driver is chromedp, not Playwright; and most of the 251 scenarios move below the browser to golden HTML and composition tests because the host renders the pages. Recordings and expected outputs are re-made in the Go formats.

The goal, exercising the real update path without release infrastructure, is kept for dsh update: its tests and scenarios run against a local or private feed with a test update key and stand-in archives (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3 and the scenarios of that specification). The mechanism described in the note (Electron's updater classes and NSIS updater in a loopback harness) has no counterpart.

The first verdict assumed a desktop updater whose observer dies when the installer replaces the application. That problem does not arise for dsh update: it is a foreground command that performs the swap, runs the new binary once with --version and reports the result itself, and it never stops the running host (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-3). Its output and exit status are the record. The note's whitelisting rule (write named fields, never raw errors or addresses) remains a rule for the crash report, which is the web host area's.

The goal, that test update material can never be offered to real clients or touch real user data, is met by a simpler mechanism: a test release is signed with a test update key, and a real binary trusts only the production key compiled into it (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-1); scenarios use a private feed and a temporary harness home. The note's random application identity and derived Electron runtime descriptors have no counterpart.

Upstream test maintenance: a repair of one Playwright scenario for a third-party React spreadsheet widget that the Go design does not use. Its lesson is general and is written into the browser lane's rules (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-6): an assertion must observe a change the action caused, never a state that was already true before it.
